questions.q: For a 4-continuous-feature dataset, how many qubits does angle encoding need versus amplitude encoding?
options: Angle encoding needs 4 qubits (one per feature); amplitude encoding needs only 2 qubits (2^2 = 4 amplitudes)
Both need exactly 4 qubits
Angle encoding needs 2 qubits; amplitude encoding needs 4 qubits
Both need exactly 2 qubits
questions.explain: Angle encoding uses one qubit per feature (4 qubits for 4 features), while amplitude encoding packs N values into log2(N) qubits, so 4 values fit into 2 qubits (2^2=4 amplitudes).

questions.q: Why can amplitude encoding's qubit-count advantage be partly or fully offset in practice, per this lesson?
options: Preparing an arbitrary normalized state can require a gate count that grows with the number of amplitudes (up to O(2^n) in the worst case), adding real noise exposure on NISQ hardware
Amplitude encoding actually requires MORE qubits than angle encoding in all cases
Amplitude encoding cannot represent continuous classical data at all
There is no offset -- amplitude encoding is strictly better in every practical case
questions.explain: While amplitude encoding needs fewer qubits, the circuit to prepare an arbitrary state on those qubits can require a gate count that grows with the number of amplitudes, which can mean more total gates (and more noise exposure) than angle encoding's simple parallel rotations.

questions.q: Under single-qubit RY angle encoding, the quantum kernel between two points x and x' works out to k(x,x') = cos^2((x-x')/2). What is k(0.4, 1.2)?
options: Approximately 0.8484
Exactly 1.0
Exactly 0
Approximately 0.4794
questions.explain: cos((0.4-1.2)/2) = cos(-0.4) is approximately 0.9211, and squaring gives approximately 0.8484, matching the direct inner-product-squared calculation.

questions.q: How does the similarity structure induced by angle encoding's kernel differ fundamentally from amplitude encoding's kernel?
options: Angle encoding's kernel is a periodic function of the feature difference, so very different feature values can map to similar kernel values; amplitude encoding's kernel is a direct cosine similarity on the raw normalized vectors with no such periodicity
They are mathematically identical regardless of encoding choice
Amplitude encoding's kernel is periodic while angle encoding's is not
Neither kernel depends on the specific encoding used
questions.explain: Angle encoding's cos^2((x-x')/2) form is periodic, meaning feature values differing by certain periodic amounts can produce the same kernel value -- a structural property with no analogue in amplitude encoding's direct cosine-similarity-on-raw-vectors structure.

questions.q: Per the lesson's practical recommendation framework, when should angle encoding typically be preferred?
options: When there are few features and shallow, easy-to-debug circuits are preferred -- which is why most labs in this course default to it
Only when the dataset has more than 1000 features
Only for strictly binary/categorical data
Angle encoding should never be used in practice according to this lesson
questions.explain: The lesson recommends angle encoding for few-feature datasets where shallow, debuggable circuits matter most -- exactly why it's the default choice across this course's labs.
